projects.title: Proof of Concept (Phase 0) Study of Clinical Trial Outcomes and Biomarkers in Early Stage Dementia with Lewy Bodies
projects.org: UNIVERSITY OF MIAMI SCHOOL OF MEDICINE
projects.abstract: ABSTRACT Approximately 1.6 million people in the United States suffer from Lewy body dementia, which includes both dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) with dementia (PDD). Unfortunately, DLB diagnoses, especially early-stage DLB (which includes DLB-MCI and mild DLB) can be difficult, with patients seeing more than 3 physicians and experiencing an 18-month delay to diagnosis with misdiagnoses commonly occurring in over 60% of cases. There are no FDA-approved treatments, greatly lagging research efforts being developed in AD and PD. At the present time, DLB diagnostic, prognostic, and theragnostic biomarkers are limited and it has been unclear as what exactly are the best clinical trial outcomes to demonstrate efficacy in a DLB trial – this has implications for the initiation and success of future DLB trials. Many commonly used dementia efficacy outcomes were developed for AD clinical trials (e.g., ADAS-Cog, ADCS-ADL), and it is uncertain how well these measures perform in DLB or what the expected annual rate of change is. There are limitations in studying mechanisms or quantifying efficacy due to the lack of biomarkers for DLB. Most studies of DLB have used biomarkers of AD (amyloid, tau) or PD (dopamine). Current markers for alpha-synuclein are qualitative (present vs absent), making them less useful as a measure of target engagement or a clinical trial outcome. To address these great unmet needs, we propose a proof-of-concept (Phase 0) study to characterize the one-year rate of change for early-stage DLB with a focus on testing the utility of two novel FDA-cleared/qualified digital assessments - Cognivue Clarity (Cognivue) and WCG’s Virtual Reality Functional Capacity Assessment Tool (VRFCAT); a new Lewy body dementia domain rating scale (LBD-DRS); and two innovative DLB biomarkers - quantitative p-synuclein129 from skin biopsies (CND Life Sciences) and multiplex proteomic profiles with NULISA (Alamar Biosciences ARGO). Our SPECIFIC AIMS are: (1) Recruit 60 early-stage, biopsy-confirmed DLB patients into a 12-month Phase 0 study with 20 age-matched healthy controls as a comparison group using standard AD and PD clinical trial measurements; (2) Test novel and innovative clinical trial outcome measures in early-stage DLB for 1-year rate of change; and (3) Identify novel biomarker patterns for clinical progression over a 1-year period. The lack of research in DLB characterization and quantitative biomarker development has hindered the development of robust clinical trials to test novel therapeutics. Findings from this study will inform the design of future clinical trials in early-stage DLB by identifying tools that could be used to assess disease progression across cognitive, functional, motor and behavioral outcomes, provide effect size estimates for proper power calculations, be sensitive to measure response to therapy, confirm target engagement, and quantify changes in alpha-synuclein in trials testing disease-modifying medications.

projects.title: Identifying and Evaluating Sensory and Motor System Changes as Biomarkers of Alzheimer’s Disease
projects.abstract: Project Summary/Abstract In the next 35 years, the prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is projected to grow rapidly, such that 14 million people in the U.S. may be diagnosed with this so-far-incurable disease. Research has shown that brain changes associated with AD and related dementias (ADRD) occur years—or possibly even a decade—before the cognitive signs that often prompt referral and diagnosis. Early identification offers the potential to stave off the illness and preserve functioning. This project’s long-term objective is to increase early identification of AD. We will do this by studying changes in a full range of sensory and motor functioning—such as olfaction, hearing, dexterity, balance, and gait—that can be observed years prior to dementia onset. The immediate goal of this research is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of sensory, motor, and cognitive tests from the NIH Toolbox as early behavioral biomarkers of AD, either on their own or in concert with molecular biomarkers that can be obtained through a blood test. This research will also help to distinguish the patterns of sensory and motor changes seen in individuals with cognitive decline from those associated with healthy cognitive aging. This proposal will leverage an existing, well-established longitudinal cohort of older individuals from a previous National Institute on Aging (NIA)-funded study known as Advancing Reliable Measurement in Alzheimer's Disease and cognitive Aging (ARMADA), who were first evaluated between 2018 and 2022. One hundred participants from the ARMADA non-dementia cohorts at the University of Michigan and the University of Wisconsin will be recruited for this study, along with an additional 300 older adults who have mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or who are otherwise at risk for developing AD. These 400 participants will be tested twice, three years apart, with measures from the NIH Toolbox (NIHTB) and the Uniform Data Set, as well as a comprehensive panel of blood-based biomarkers (BBB) of pathological tau and amyloid, genetic risk for AD, protein markers of synucleinopathies, as well as synaptic and neuronal network dysfunction, inflammation, and neuronal cell death. This work will have a significant impact on utilizing sensory, motor, and cognitive tests as non-invasive biomarkers for early identification of AD, as well as understanding changes in sensory and motor systems in MCI/dementia vs. healthy cognitive aging. This proposal has three specific aims: Aim 1: Evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of accessible sensory, motor, and cognitive tests as early behavioral biomarkers of AD; Aim 2: Identify a combined molecular-behavioral biomarker battery for prediction of AD from the NIHTB sensory, motor, and cognitive tests together with BBB of AD pathology; and Aim 3: Investigate the patterns and timing of sensory and motor changes in older adults with and without cognitive impairment. This proposal is directly responsive to the NIA’s Notice of Special Interest: Sensory and Motor System Changes as Predictors of Preclinical Alzheimer’s Disease (NOT-AG-21-044).

projects.title: Cognitive SuperAging: A model to explore resilience and resistance to aging and Alzheimers disease
projects.abstract: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT Aging is the greatest risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and memory complaints are among the most common concerns reported by older adults. However, not all aging trajectories are marked by decline. SuperAgers (individuals aged 80 and above with episodic memory performance comparable to individuals in their 50s and 60s) represent a rare and informative phenotype of successful cognitive aging. This project builds on over 15 years of our work, including the establishment of the first SuperAging cohort with longitudinal follow- up and brain donation. Prior findings demonstrated that SuperAgers exhibit youthful cortical integrity, particularly in the anterior cingulate, lower cortical AD pathology, an abundance of Von Economo neurons, and unique psychosocial and genetic features. Despite these discoveries, the functional mechanisms supporting this exceptional memory performance remain incompletely understood, and broader recruitment is needed to enhance generalizability and discovery of other potentially modifiable factors. The project will expand the geographic reach of identifying and enrolling SuperAgers and Controls through a new Digital Cohort. The project proposes targeted, hypothesis-driven approaches to address current gaps. Aim 1 will leverage an ecologically valid functional MRI task to examine neural mechanisms underlying superior memory performance. Aim 2 will identify SuperAging protective features using genome-wide SNPs. Aim 3 will assess how long-term, mid-to-late- life outdoor exposures (e.g., particulate air pollution, PM2.5) are related to SuperAging using validated methodologies. This project will integrate cognitive, imaging, genetic, and environmental data to identify protective and potentially modifiable factors associated with exceptional cognitive aging. By expanding the cohort through the application of novel digital recruitment methods, and targeting real-world exposures, this research will provide insights into the biology of cognitive resilience and resistance. The outcomes have high potential for translation to AD and related dementias (ADRD) prevention and healthspan promotion. The project’s reliance on a cohort that has already been partially recruited, its longitudinal design, multidisciplinary structure, and collaboration-friendly organization increase the likelihood that consequential progress will be achieved.

projects.title: Investigating the Role of Gustatory Cortical Dynamics in Foraging Behaviors
projects.abstract: Project Summary This project addresses a fundamental question in neuroscience: how does the brain integrate sensory experience into memory systems to support adaptive behavior? Although the hippocampus is widely recognized as a cognitive map, it remains unclear what features of experience are incorporated into this representation and why certain variables are prioritized. In natural behavior, animals navigate environments containing stimuli that differ in biological significance, particularly those related to survival and fitness. This work focuses on taste as a model system for studying how biologically meaningful sensory information becomes integrated into hippocampal representations. Taste is inherently evaluative, signaling whether stimuli should be approached or avoided. Prior work demonstrates that hippocampal neurons encode taste information in a spatially gated manner, suggesting that evaluative sensory signals are incorporated into spatial memory. However, the circuit mechanisms underlying this integration and its role in guiding behavior remain poorly understood. The proposed studies will test the hypothesis that gustatory cortical input provides decision-relevant evaluative signals that support the formation and updating of taste–place associations in the hippocampus. This will be accomplished using a novel open-field foraging task in which animals learn and update associations between spatial locations and tastants, combined with temporally specific optogenetic perturbation of gustatory cortical activity. Behavioral analyses will quantify learning, flexibility, and foraging efficiency to determine how disruption of taste-related signals affects memory-guided behavior. This fellowship will provide interdisciplinary training in systems neuroscience, including behavioral task design, circuit-level manipulation, and quantitative analysis of complex behavior. Training will be conducted in the laboratory of Dr. Donald Katz, which provides expertise in taste processing, sensory coding, and behavior, and in close collaboration with Dr. Shantanu Jadhav, whose laboratory offers advanced training in hippocampal systems neuroscience and circuit-level analysis. The research environment includes access to state-of-the-art behavioral and electrophysiological platforms, high-channel-count neural recording systems, flexible maze systems, and advanced computational infrastructure for large-scale data analysis . The broader Brandeis neuroscience community provides a highly collaborative and multidisciplinary training environment, with extensive opportunities for scientific exchange through seminars, journal clubs, and cross- laboratory interactions. Together, this integrated training plan and environment will support the development of a research program focused on how biologically meaningful sensory information shapes memory systems and adaptive behavior.

projects.title: Integration of Duplicated Odorant Receptors into Ant Olfactory Circuits
projects.abstract: Project Summary The ability to detect chemical cues and use them to guide behavior is fundamental across animals. Canonically, olfactory sensory neurons in the periphery express a single odorant receptor (OR) and converge with neurons expressing the same receptor onto shared glomerular targets in the central brain. How this conserved architecture accommodates rapid expansion of receptor repertoires remains poorly understood. The clonal raider ant, Ooceraea biroi, provides a tractable system to address this question because it relies on chemical communication to coordinate social behavior and has approximately 500 ORs and a corresponding number of olfactory glomeruli, nearly an order of magnitude more than the fruit fly. This project tests the hypothesis that expanded OR repertoires are accommodated by regulatory and circuit mechanisms that preserve singular receptor choice while enabling the emergence of new sensory neuron classes and glomerular targets. Two integrated aims will define how recently duplicated ORs are incorporated into existing olfactory circuits. Aim 1 will determine whether duplicated ORs achieve mutually exclusive expression and will map their spatial distribution across the adult antenna. Aim 2 will model gene duplication by introducing endogenous OR duplicates and exogenous ORs into the genome, then test whether these receptors are singularly expressed, spatially restricted, and sufficient to generate new functional glomeruli. This project will be carried out in the laboratory of Dr. Daniel Kronauer at Rockefeller University, which provides an exceptional environment for studying chemosensation, gene duplication, and neural circuit organization. The work will provide advanced training in two-photon imaging, olfactometry, and quantitative image analysis, while strengthening skills in scientific communication, mentorship, and independent project development. This research will define mechanisms by which expanded chemosensory receptor repertoires are integrated into functional olfactory circuits. By revealing how a sensory system specialized for chemical communication accommodates genomic change, the project will advance general principles of sensory circuit assembly, gene regulation, and sensory system evolution relevant to biomedical science.

projects.title: Peripheral mechanisms of Temporomandibular joint pain
projects.abstract: Temporomandibular joint and muscle disorders (TMDs) is the most prevalent orofacial pain conditions that involve the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), masticatory muscles, and associated head and neck musculoskeletal structures. Patients with TMD suffer from myofascial pain, limited mandibular motion, and TMJ sounds. Among U.S. adults about 5-25% and among them over 10 million suffer from TMJ pain and resulting severe psychosocial and economic burden is more than $30 billion per year. However, we do not know the exact mechanisms for TMD and TMJ pain. Thus, in order to better serve TMD patients, it is necessary to better understand the mechanisms of TMJ pain. In particular, it is not known exactly how spontaneous or ongoing pain occurs in TMJ pain patients. It also remains unclear what pinpointing molecules that lead to chronic, persistent jaw joint and muscle pain at the level of the primary sensory neuron. Although there is much research on individual sensory neurons and its hypersensitivity mechanisms, we still do not understand how in vivo trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons function at a populational ensemble under physiological and disease conditions, due to the lack of proper tools and techniques. In addition, we have been unable to directly monitor and visualize the many subtypes and specific sensory modalities of in vivo TG sensory neurons. In this proposal, we will take novel approaches to overcome these obstacles by combining state-of-the art in vivo TG Pirt-GCaMP3 Ca2+ imaging as recently developed by us, patch recording, and newly developed modality specific transgenic mouse lines. We have expanded our imaging mouse-genetic toolbox that enable simultaneous visualization of all four LTMR subtypes; Aβ SA-LTMRs, Aβ RA-LTMRs, Aδ-LTMRs, and C-LTMRs and selectively label peptidergic and non- peptidergic nociceptors. Specific labeling of distinct sensory neuron subtypes provides an unprecedented opportunity to determine whether the activity of each subtype is altered during chronic TMJ pain. In this way, we are capable of analyzing neuronal Ca2+ activity over 2800 TG neurons simultaneously. Using this powerful technique and tools, we discovered a neuronal network activity, which we term “spontaneous activation”, in which neurons activate themselves without any stimuli following TMJ pain that is not seen in naïve animals. This spontaneous activation occurs in various sizes of neurons including small-diameter nociceptors and large- diameter LTMRs. Combining the imaging technique with pharmacological and genetic approaches, we discovered that spontaneous activation is induced by an upregulation of metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) in TG neurons after TMJ pain. Blocking mGluR5 significantly attenuated neuronal spontaneous activation and also reduced mechanical hypersensitivity. Therefore, our central hypothesis is that spontaneous activation is a mechanism for ongoing pain of TMJ pain patients as a form of neuronal plasticity and thus that spontaneously activated neurons via mGluR5 signal neighboring neurons, specifically pain-transmitting neurons, thus it contributes to TMJ hypersensitivity.

projects.title: SN102: a Novel Gene Therapy for Trigeminal Neuralgia Pain
projects.abstract: ABSTRACT Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a severe neuropathic pain condition affecting up to 15,000 new patients annually in the US. Current treatments are limited to medications with serious side effects and poor efficacy, or invasive neurosurgical procedures. SN102 is a novel gene therapy that utilizes base editing to install a naturally occurring pain-dampening allele specifically in peripheral pain-sensing neurons, offering the potential for safe and durable pain relief through a single treatment via local injection. Importantly, our preliminary data demonstrate SN102's sustained efficacy in mouse osteoarthritis (OA) pain models for up to 10 weeks, providing strong proof-of- concept. The goal of this Phase I SBIR project is to optimize SN102's delivery system for peripheral nervous system (PNS) specificity and demonstrate its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors through the following specific aims. In Aim 1, we will quantify the baseline efficacy of SN102 using AAV-PHP.S, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid variant with enhanced peripheral neuron tropism, by examining calcium transients in edited iPSC-nociceptors at varying multiplicities of infection to establish the relationship between gene editor expression and functional outcomes. In Aim 2, we will optimize SN102 for PNS specificity by conducting an in silico screen of nociceptor-specific regulatory elements. In Aim 3, we will evaluate the top regulatory element candidates identified by the screen across multiple iPSC-derived cell types to confirm improved PNS specificity and efficacy of the optimized SN102 in human iPSC-nociceptors. Success in these studies will establish the foundational work for SN102 as a transformative therapy for TN patients and support advancement toward in vivo studies in a subsequent Phase II SBIR, with potential applications across multiple chronic pain conditions.

projects.title: Generation of a CCL2-CGRP bispecific neutralizing antibody to treat chronic post-traumatic headache
projects.abstract: Project Summary/Abstract Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is the most common and persistent consequence of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), affecting millions of Americans every year. Despite its prevalence and disabling impact, there is no approved treatment specifically for chronic PTH. Many patients use/misuse opioids, which heightens the risk of addiction and overdose death, underscoring the urgent need for safe and effective non-opioid therapies. Although both clinical and animal studies implicates both neuropeptide CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) and chemokine C-C motif ligand 2 (CCL2) signaling in the pathogenesis of chronic PTH, inhibiting either pathway alone only protects mice against some PTH triggers and not the others. Remarkably, our preliminary data demonstrate that dual blockade of CGRP and CCL2 signaling fully prevented chronic PTH- related behavioral sensitization in mice across multiple clinically relevant PTH triggers, establishing a strong scientific premise for a combinatorial approach. We propose to develop a first-in-class bispecific antibody (BsAb) that simultaneously neutralizes CCL2 and CGRP as a novel non-opioid treatment for chronic PTH. In the R61 phase, we will generate chimeric neutralizing Abs against human CGRP and CCL2. Single- chain variable fragment (scFv) phage display libraries will be constructed with RNA from splenocytes of immunized rabbits. Customized panning will be conducted to select phages that show strong and selective antigen binding at pH 7.4 but weaker binding at pH 5.8, aiming to facilitate antigen clearance. After converting scFvs to chimeric Abs, we will screen for Abs that bind to human and mouse antigens with high affinity, and robustly neutralize their functions. After confirming that the combination treatment is superior to single Ab administration in a mouse model of chronic PTH, we will select one anti-CGRP and two anti-CCL2 chimeric Abs that bind to distinct epitopes on human CCL2 for the R33 phase. In the R33 phase, we will first humanize the top chimeric Abs to retain all desired features. Next, we will engineer multiple BsAb configurations with the anti-CCL2 arm in biparatopic format to further enhance antigen clearance. Top BsAb will be selected based on the binding affinity, neutralizing ability to human and mouse antigens, and drug-like properties. Last, initial in vivo pharmacokinetic study will be performed to assess the blood half-life, the levels in dura and trigeminal ganglion tissues and the efficiency of BsAb-antigen complex clearance. The therapeutic efficacy of the top BsAb will be assessed in the mouse model of chronic PTH to see if it matches or exceeds the efficacy of the combination of humanized Abs and outperforms monotherapies. Upon completion of the project, we will obtain a humanized CCL2-CGRP neutralizing BsAb with enhanced antigen clearance and validated preclinical efficacy, ready for advancing to the Blueprint Neurotherapeutics Network for Biologic-based Drugs. All in all, this project will deliver a novel, non-opioid therapeutic strategy for chronic PTH, addressing a major public health burden and transforming care for patients with mTBI.

projects.title: Mechanism-guided amelioration of hyperactivity in human and rodent nociceptors linked to spontaneous pain
projects.pis: Alexis Guillaume Bavencoffe; Patrick M Dougherty; EDGAR T. WALTERS
projects.org: UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS HLTH SCI CTR HOUSTON
projects.abstract: Project Summary The long-term objective of this project is to discover novel, highly targeted approaches for treating ongoing or spontaneous human pain that minimizes adverse side effects. It builds on accumulating evidence that ongoing pain is driven – to a far greater extent than previously recognized – by persistent spontaneous or ongoing electrical activity generated in sensory neurons that detect injury and inflammation, nociceptors. This ongoing activity (OA) is termed spontaneous activity (SA) when generated by mechanisms intrinsic to an active neuron, and OA more generally (e.g., when persistent activity is driven by prolonged exposure to inflammatory mediators). In many cases, including in human patients with neuropathic pain, pain-associated OA is generated in the nociceptor cell body (soma). Fortuitously, somally generated OA induced by painful conditions in a person or rodent can persist after isolation of the nociceptor soma (removing it from the body and ganglion), and it is evident during recording with whole-cell patch clamp methods. These recordings reveal irregular, depolarizing spontaneous fluctuations of membrane potential (DSFs) that are critical for controlling the likelihood and pattern of OA induced by neuropathic conditions, surgical injury, and inflammation. This project extends recent progress defining the contributions of multiple ion channels to the generation of large DSFs that control the likelihood and pattern of OA. It will test the hypothesis that specific ion channels – including Nav1.8 and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) – that are important for generating large DSFs and hyperexcitability can be targeted together by combinations of low concentrations of clinically relevant inhibitors to reduce ongoing pain. Mechanism-based predictions of this hypothesis will be tested using selected drugs and hyperactive human nociceptors. Drugs, including two that are FDA-approved for other uses and that have mechanisms of action that should reduce large DSFs and OA in nociceptors, will be tested with customized whole-cell patch methods on dorsal root ganglion neurons isolated from cancer patients with documented neuropathic pain distributions. The effects of a wide range of doses of ion channel blockers will be examined individually and in combination. In parallel studies, the prediction that combined blockers of Nav1.8 and VGCCs will suppress ongoing pain behavior will be tested using three quite different rodent models of clinically significant pain in which potentiation of DSFs and SA/OA is prominently involved: a central neuropathy model (rat spinal cord injury), a postsurgical pain model (rat extended plantar incision), and a chemotherapy model (mouse cisplatin treatment). This project will leverage basic knowledge about DSFs (a particularly important driver of pain-associated OA in nociceptors) to select and test novel drug combinations that offer promise for the improved treatment of spontaneous and ongoing pain.

projects.title: Neuroendocrine mechanisms of female chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPC)
projects.abstract: Project Summary Women have a higher prevalence of chronic pain than men and often suffer from multiple chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPC). Mechanisms promoting COPCs in women are not well understood. COPCs typically peak during reproductive age, are exacerbated by stress or during the menstrual cycle, suggesting that stress- related female hormones may promote female pain and increase the co-occurrence of two or more chronic pain diseases. Endometriosis is a gynecological condition characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. Women with endometriosis experience pelvic pain and are twice as likely to have comorbid migraine. Endometriosis and migraine patients have high levels of circulating prolactin (PRL), a female predominant neurohormone. PRL is under dual control by stress and estrogen and is released primarily from the anterior pituitary and from other tissues including endometrium. PRL selectively sensitizes nociceptors from female rodents, non-human primates and human organ donors suggesting that this evolutionarily conserved neuroendocrine mechanism is relevant to multiple female pain conditions. We propose to investigate the role of PRL and its receptor (PRLR) in endometriosis-associated pelvic pain and endometriosis-induced comorbid migraine pain. Pelvic and migraine-like pain behaviors will be assessed in a syngeneic mouse model of endometriosis to determine the contributions of pituitary PRL as well as locally secreted PRL from endometriotic lesions. We hypothesize that dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons that innervate pelvic structures and trigeminal ganglion (TG) neurons will be sensitized in endometriosis mice, promoting, respectively, endometriosis-associated pelvic pain and increased vulnerability to migraine-like pain. Possible PRL/PRLR-induced neural adaptations in DRG and TG neurons that may underlie the comorbidity of endometriosis and migraine pain will be explored using genetic, transcriptomic (spatial transcriptomics), electrophysiolgical and microscopic techniques. We will also evaluate whether neutralization of PRL with a novel, first-in-class human PRL monoclonal antibody (hPRL-mAb) can block both DRG and TG sensitization and relieve endometriosis-induced pelvic pain and comorbid migraine pain. These studies aim to unravel a neuroendocrine mechanism that may promote widespread sensitivity to pain in women as a basis for development of chronic overlapping pain conditions. Identification of high PRL levels as a contributing factor to COPCs could improve personalized medicine by facilitating early detection, diagnosis and treatment of diseases that primarily affect women or are female specific. Evaluation of the efficacy of hPRL-mAb for the treatment of endometriosis-associated abdominal pain and comorbid migraine will stimulate the advancement of new therapeutic approaches such as hPRL-mAbs specifically tailored for treatment of pain in women. Better treatment options targeting female prevalent COPCs will address the health disparities in women.
